title: How to Avoid Burnout in Ministry
subtitle: The causes, the warning signs, and the slow recovery of a pastor who ran himself empty in the name of faithfulness and called it obedience.

sections.title: Burnout Is Devotion That Forgot to Stop
sections.body:
No one collapses doing what they despise. They collapse doing what they love, far past the point where love was meant to rest. That is the trap. Burnout does not arrive dressed as sin. It arrives dressed as commitment, and the church applauds the costume right up until the man inside it falls.

I know the early causes because I supplied them myself. A schedule with no edges. A phone that never went dark. A quiet belief that the church was held up by my effort and would sink without it. That last one is the root. It looks like zeal and it is actually a small atheism, a conviction that God will not keep his house unless I never sleep.

Not all of my exhaustion was love. Some of it was fear of being seen as lazy. Some of it was the pleasure of being needed. I dressed all of it in the language of sacrifice, because no one rebukes a pastor for working too hard for Jesus. They thank him. They hand him toward the cliff with gratitude on their faces.

sections.title: The Body and the Soul Both Send Warnings
sections.body:
Burnout announces itself long before it arrives. The trouble is that a busy man reads the warnings as character flaws to overcome rather than alarms to obey.

The first sign is cynicism toward the people you once loved to serve. They become interruptions. Their needs become weights. You catch yourself resenting the very sheep you were ordained to feed. The second sign is a short fuse at home, because the public self is held together by force and the private self is where the cost gets paid. Your family meets the man your congregation never sees.

The third sign is the death of joy in prayer. You still talk, but the line feels dead. You preach about a nearness you have stopped feeling. And the fourth is dread, a low Sunday dread that sits in the stomach on Friday and grows. When those four are present together, you are not weak. You are warned. A warning ignored is not courage. It is the engine seizing because the driver refused to read the dashboard.

sections.title: What You Believe About God When You Will Not Rest
sections.body:
Underneath every burned-out pastor is a theology he would never say out loud. He believes the work is finally his. He believes the results depend on his output. He believes that if he stops, something will fall, and he is too afraid of the falling to test whether God might catch it.

God commanded rest, and he commanded it with a threat, because he knew we would not take it otherwise. The Sabbath was not a reward for the productive. It was a weekly confession that the world runs without us. A man who refuses it is not more faithful. He is announcing, with his body, that he does not trust the One he preaches.

Jesus withdrew while people were still sick. The crowds pressed and he went to the mountain to pray, and he let real need go unmet so he could attend to his own soul before the Father. He did it without apology. The pastor who cannot do that has confused himself with the Messiah, and it is the most tiring heresy there is.

sections.title: How a Burned Man Comes Back
sections.body:
Recovery is slower than the collapse, and that humbles you. You spent years digging the hole. You will not climb out in a weekend retreat.

It begins with confession, not to the congregation but to God and to two or three people who will tell you the truth. You name the idol. You say it plainly. I believed the church needed me more than it needed God. Until that sentence is spoken, every rest you take will feel like guilt rather than obedience.

Then comes rebuilding rhythm. A real day off, defended like a marriage. Sleep treated as a spiritual discipline rather than a sign of weakness. Work given away, even to people who will do it worse than you, because done worse by another beats done well by a man in the ground. And slowly, the joy returns, not as a reward you earned but as a gift you stopped blocking. The dead line in prayer comes back to life. The dread lifts. You learn the difference between a poured-out life and a bled-out one, and you guard it for the rest of your ministry.

sections.title: The Man Who Would Not Read the Signs
sections.body:
I buried a friend who would not read the signs. Good pastor, real gift, beloved by his people. He worked the way I once worked, and the church grew, and everyone praised his stamina. His heart gave out at fifty-eight after years of warnings he treated as suggestions.

They called him a faithful servant who gave everything for the kingdom. I sat there and could not say amen. He did not give everything for the kingdom. He gave everything because he could not trust the kingdom to stand without him. He gave his wife a husband she barely saw and his children a father made of fatigue, and we called it sacrifice because his ruin matched our picture of a hero.

I am not sure I would have done better. That is why I write this with my own warning lights in view. The tired shepherd does not need another sermon on working harder. He needs permission, in the name of the God who rested, to stop before he is taken.

Stop now. Not after the collapse. The God you serve already finished the work you are killing yourself to complete.
